text: The Navajo call themselves Diné, “the people”, and their ancestors are believed to have come south from Canada and Alaska.
From the Pueblo peoples they learned to farm corn, beans and squash.
src: The Navajo call themselves Diné, “the people” / their ancestors are believed to have migrated from northwestern Canada and eastern Alaska / A southward migration of Athabaskan peoples from subarctic North America dated to around 1,000 years ago
They later took up farming from the Pueblo peoples, growing the “Three Sisters” of corn, beans and squash

text: They also learned to weave cotton on upright looms from the Pueblo peoples.
From the Spanish came sheep and goats, and Navajo women wove the wool into blankets that people valued and traded.
src: learned to weave cotton on upright looms from the Pueblo peoples
herding sheep and goats from the Spanish / Navajo women spun and wove wool into blankets and clothing that were highly valued and traded

text: Weavers added red yarn and blue indigo dye to their black, grey and white wool, making fine striped blankets.
Silverwork is an important Navajo art too, with necklaces, bracelets and belts.
src: they added imported red bayeta yarn and indigo to their black, grey and white wool, and their fine Chief’s Blankets, striped in three phases of growing pattern
Silversmithing is an important art / bracelets, necklaces and bracers / the concha belt

text: In 1864 the US Army forced around 9,000 Navajo men, women and children on the Long Walk to Bosque Redondo.
Many suffered there from disease and cold, and in 1868 the survivors could return to part of their homeland.
src: 1864: The US Army forces around 9,000 Navajo men, women and children on the Long Walk of over 300 miles to internment at Bosque Redondo
where crop failure, disease, cold and raids made the internment a disaster / the treaty of 1868 let the survivors return to part of their homeland

text: During the Second World War, Navajo code talkers used their own language as a secret code, which the Japanese never cracked.
Today the Navajo Nation has more than 400,000 citizens and the largest reservation in the United States.
src: During the Second World War up to four hundred Navajo code talkers carried messages for the US Marine Corps in a code built on their own language / the Japanese never deciphered it
With more than 427,414 enrolled citizens in 2026 / which grew into the largest reservation in the United States
